claim: lavahq.io and lavalabs.io are the same company: lavalabs.io returns HTTP 301 to lavahq.io, and the GitHub org 'lava-security-research' lists its website as https://lavahq.io and its contact email as research@lavalabs.io
design_impact: Establishes a single confirmed identity for all lavahq.io/lavalabs.io facts; both domains may be cited interchangeably for this entity only.

claim: lavahq.io's public homepage is marked 'Coming soon' and reads 'Security for Enterprise Data Centers and Neoclouds'; the only visible compliance marker is 'ISO 27001 Certified'
design_impact: Confirms Lava is pre-launch/stealth on its actual product; public surface is dominated by research content, not product documentation.

claim: Lava's About page states: 'Lava is built by infrastructure engineers and security experts with a track record of building enterprise products for mission-critical environments. We focus on the layers that are hardest to manage, secure, and control.'
design_impact: Supports positioning Lava as an infra-security company targeting the hardest-to-reach layers (firmware, BMC, management plane) rather than app-layer security.

claim: None of the 17 pages reached in the bounded, sitemap-complete crawl of lavahq.io contain the phrases 'tens of thousands', 'central plane', or 'no way in, only a way out' (or close paraphrases) describing a deployed sensor fleet
design_impact: The internal brief's specific sensor/fleet/one-way-out framing is NOT publicly confirmed; treat it as either forward-looking/unreleased product language or paraphrase from a non-public source. Do not present the brief's exact wording as independently verified from the public web.

claim: Lava's flagship public research (published ~2026-07-28) scanned the public internet and found 36,872 internet-exposed IPMI/BMC hosts on UDP/623, of which 24,650 (66.9%) disclosed password-derived RAKP authentication hashes pre-login via CVE-2013-4786 (a 2004-era IPMI 2.0 flaw); Lava built an interactive 'BMCRadar' map of the exposure and reported findings responsibly to Supermicro and HPE
design_impact: This is Lava's single most publicized piece of research and directly supports ranking a BMC/IPMI exposure-and-hardening health check highly.

claim: Lava published 'FORGE: A Practical Security Framework for Data Centers and AI Infrastructure' (GitHub lava-security-research/forge-framework, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, 20 stars), organized into five pillars: Fleet Integrity, Operations & Management Planes, Resource Isolation, Grid, and Evidence & Exposure Management; authored by Michael Katchinskiy (Head of Security Research) and Yakir Kadkoda (CTO/co-founder), reviewed by named experts from Google, Dell, Nebius, Roblox, IBM, Intel, and Visa
design_impact: FORGE's five pillars are the clearest public statement of what Lava considers the taxonomy of data-center/AI-infra risk and are a direct blueprint for prioritizing which custom health-check category signals engineering judgment to a Lava-aligned reader.

claim: Lava's three-part 'Breaking the Trust' blog series covers firmware integrity fundamentals (chain of trust, SPDM, CoRIM, External Root of Trust), real-world firmware compromise (MoonBounce, LoJax, BlackLotus, iLOBleed, MegaRAC, CosmicStrand), and enforcement practice (attestation over self-reported inventory)
design_impact: Strong public evidence that Secure Boot state, TPM presence, kernel taint/unsigned-module status, and firmware self-report vs. attestation gaps are exactly the class of finding Lava's own research treats as foundational (Fleet Integrity pillar).

claim: Lava's three-part 'runtime integrity' blog series covers kernel rootkits (Diamorphine, Drovorub, LinkPro, BPFDoor), eBPF-based backdoors, LD_PRELOAD/user-space rootkits (Azazel, Symbiote), and mitigations including kernel module signing, kernel lockdown modes, eBPF-loading restriction, and continuous runtime verification ('soft purge' vs 'hard purge')
design_impact: Strong public evidence supporting a kernel/runtime-hardening health check category (lockdown mode, module-signing enforcement, ptrace_scope/kptr_restrict/dmesg_restrict/unprivileged_bpf_disabled sysctls, unexpected-taint detection).

claim: Lava's neocloud/shared-responsibility posts explicitly name 'storage media sanitization,' 'hardware and device lifecycle... reuse, decommissioning,' 'GPU state cleanup between workloads,' and ask 'what happens to a bare-metal machine before it moves from one customer to another?' as customer-relevant infrastructure concerns providers should make visible
design_impact: Direct textual support for a storage-reuse/data-remnant health-check category, even outside strict multi-tenancy, since bare-metal-as-a-service providers (like the Lava host's own Latitude.sh) reuse physical nodes between customers by the same logic Lava describes.

claim: Lava's only public GitHub repository (forge-framework) contains Markdown documentation and images only -- no source code, no language runtime, and no mention of Go, Python, or any specific sensor implementation stack
design_impact: No public evidence exists to inform or override the sensor's own implementation-language choice (Go, per this project's design); Lava's public GitHub presence gives risk taxonomy, not engineering-stack signal.

claim: The bounded, sitemap-complete crawl (17 of 18 sitemap URLs successfully fetched) found no /careers or /jobs page and no linked external ATS (Greenhouse/Lever/Ashby/Breezy); the About page's only hiring-relevant text is 'We're scaling fast... always looking for top-tier talent'
design_impact: Cannot verify the hiring-stack question (Go? BMC/Redfish? storage?) from job postings; this is a genuine public-research gap, not a contradiction -- recorded rather than guessed.

claim: A WebSearch for 'lavahq.io careers jobs' surfaced a DIFFERENT company also named 'Lava' -- an AI-monetization/payments platform with products called 'Build' and 'Gateway', a careers portal at lava.breezy.hr, and a reported $5.8M raised -- that is NOT lavahq.io/lavalabs.io and shares no confirmed link to it
design_impact: Identity-confusion risk realized and caught: none of the payments-company facts (funding figure, product names, career portal) are attributed to lavahq.io in any other artifact in this brief.

claim: Multiple additional companies/products named 'Lava' exist and are confirmed distinct from lavahq.io: Lava Network (blockchain RPC infrastructure, ~$27M raised across rounds, founders Yair Cleper and Gil Binder), Lava International (Indian phone manufacturer), Lavastorm Analytics (legacy data-analytics vendor), Lavaan (R statistics package), LAVA VC (venture fund), LAVA Technology Services, and LAVA Laboratory for Visionary Architecture (architecture firm)
design_impact: Establishes the disambiguation baseline referenced by every other claim in this brief; none of these entities' facts are merged into lavahq.io claims.

claim: Lava frames its target reader/customer as data-center operators, neocloud/GPU-cloud providers, and infrastructure/security leadership: FORGE was 'built with CISOs, neocloud experts, researchers, and infrastructure leaders', and research posts close with 'If your organization operates data centers or AI, GPU, or bare-metal infrastructure, we'd be happy to speak with you'
design_impact: Supports writing findings evidence in a register legible to CISOs/infrastructure leaders (concrete counts, named CVEs, remediation steps) rather than a pure developer debug log.

claim: Lava's own research writing consistently (a) cites a specific CVE ID, (b) quantifies findings numerically, (c) names vendors and disclosure timelines, and (d) explicitly states ethical/scope boundaries ('We did not submit the matching passwords... or use them to authenticate')
design_impact: The sensor's own findings.json evidence strings should mirror this concrete, boundary-explicit style -- exact paths/exit-codes/errno and an explicit statement of what was NOT done (no writes, no auth attempts) -- to read as credible to this audience.

claim: FORGE's fifth pillar, 'Evidence & Exposure Management', is explicitly defined around 'provider transparency and patch velocity'
design_impact: Directly supports a firmware/kernel staleness-and-patch-velocity health-check category (installed vs. running kernel, BIOS/firmware version currency) as on-thesis for Lava's own stated framework.

claim: (Host cross-reference, not a public-web claim) Per state/HOST_SNAPSHOT.json, the target host's BMC is reachable only via an in-band KCS interface (root-only /dev/ipmi0) and a USB-gadget out-of-band NIC that is currently DOWN and unaddressed -- i.e., unlike the internet-exposed IPMI-over-LAN hosts in Lava's own BMC research, this specific host's BMC is not network-reachable at scan time
design_impact: A literal 'is IPMI reachable on UDP/623' check would report PASS/not-applicable on this host; the more valuable check here is BMC *posture* (firmware/manufacturer metadata, interface state, credential-rotation evidence where readable) rather than exposure, since exposure itself is absent on this host.

claim: Public professional roles confirmed: Michael Katchinskiy holds the title 'Head of Security Research' at Lava; Yakir Kadkoda holds the title 'CTO' / 'CTO and Co-Founder' at Lava, per the FORGE repository's authorship credit and independent search-result snippets
design_impact: Named individuals recorded in public-professional-role form only (name + title + public work claim), per the personal-data-collection limit in this track's constraints; no further personal detail sought or recorded.

claim: No funding round, investor, or valuation figure specifically attributable to lavahq.io/lavalabs.io (the data-center-security company) was found in public search results; all 'Lava... funding' search results resolve to Lava Network (blockchain RPC infrastructure, distinct founders and investors)
design_impact: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence for a pre-launch/stealth company; funding status of lavahq.io itself remains genuinely unknown and is not guessed at.
